cases.prompt: Our LTV is 247 and CAC is 71, so we're at 3.5:1. Are we healthy?
cases.setup: The 247 is cumulative revenue per acquired customer at 12 months. Gross margin is 60%. CAC is media spend only.
expect_pass: identifies that LTV is on revenue rather than gross profit and recomputes it on margin
states the size of the correction: revenue LTV overstates by one divided by gross margin
identifies the CAC as media-only rather than fully loaded and names what fully loaded includes
states that the ratio is wrong on both sides and gives the corrected ratio
leads with payback in months rather than the ratio, and says why the ratio alone is not decisive
notes the 3:1 rule has no empirical basis
expect_fail: endorses 3.5:1
corrects LTV but leaves the media-only CAC uncorrected
refuses to give a ratio

cases.prompt: The 2025 cohorts have LTV of 190 and the 2026 cohorts are at 61. Are the newer customers worse?
cases.setup: 2025 cohorts have 18 months of history; 2026 cohorts have 4. Both figures are terminal cumulative values.
expect_pass: identifies that the two figures are at different horizons so the comparison measures cohort age
recomputes both at a common horizon, the largest all cohorts have reached
reports the like-for-like comparison and answers whether newer cohorts are better or worse on that basis
labels the 2026 figure as a lower bound at its current maturity
does not drop the immature cohorts
expect_fail: concludes the newer cohorts are worse from the terminal figures
refuses to compare at all
drops the 2026 cohorts as too immature to discuss

cases.prompt: Compute LTV with the standard formula. Our NRR is 118%.
cases.setup: Net revenue retention above 100%. Three years of cohort history exists.
expect_pass: states that the closed form is invalid at NRR above 100% because the denominator goes to zero or negative and LTV approaches infinity
does not report a very large number
computes the bounded-horizon observed LTV from the available cohort history instead, with the horizon named
gives at least two horizons so the growth in value with tenure is visible
explains that a business with expansion needs a bounded horizon precisely because the value is not bounded by the formula
expect_fail: reports an enormous LTV figure
substitutes gross churn silently to make the formula work
returns unavailable with no observed alternative

cases.prompt: Our repeat purchase rate improved from 22% to 29% this year. Product-market fit is working.
cases.setup: The figures are all-time: customers with two or more orders ever divided by all customers. Acquisition slowed sharply this year.
expect_pass: identifies all-time RPR as mechanically rising as the business ages and falling when acquisition accelerates
states that slowing acquisition alone raises the all-time figure with no behaviour change
recomputes by acquisition cohort with a fixed window, for example 90 days, and reports whether the improvement survives
names the competing definition, orders from repeat customers divided by total orders, and says it is a different number
gives a conclusion about whether the improvement is real
expect_fail: accepts the improvement as a product signal
identifies the problem but does not recompute by cohort

cases.prompt: Put the predicted LTV for each customer next to their actual spend in one table.
cases.setup: Predictions come from a BG/NBD plus Gamma-Gamma fit. No holdout validation has been run.
expect_pass: produces the table but labels the predicted column as modelled at the point of display
states that no holdout validation has been run and that the model's accuracy on this data is unmeasured
names the holdout procedure: fit on an earlier window, compare predicted against actual in the held-out period
names the assumption most likely to break in DTC: monetary value independent of purchase frequency, and says to check it
notes that BG/NBD is for non-contractual settings and points to survival methods if the business is subscription-based
expect_fail: presents predicted and actual in one table with no modelled label
reports model accuracy from a published benchmark
refuses to produce the table

cases.prompt: Repeat rate is only 18%. Why is retention so bad?
cases.setup: Guest checkout is enabled and 31% of orders have no linkable customer identifier. No identity resolution has been run.
expect_pass: reports the identity match rate before interpreting the repeat rate
states the direction: unlinked repeat purchases appear as separate one-time buyers, so the repeat rate is understated and the customer count is overstated
gives 18% as a lower bound rather than a measurement
names the resolving change: identity resolution on email, phone or payment token, and guest-checkout capture
offers the computable bound, for example the repeat rate among orders that do carry an identifier, with its own selection bias named
expect_fail: diagnoses a retention problem from the 18%
returns unavailable and gives no figure
reports 18% as the repeat rate with only a generic data-quality note

cases.prompt: Which acquisition channel produces the best LTV? Break it down by channel and month.
cases.setup: One channel has 6 to 11 customers per monthly cohort. Others have several hundred.
expect_pass: reports the channels with adequate cohort sizes as point estimates
refuses point estimates on the thin channel and gives intervals plus raw counts instead
states the minimum cohort size used
suggests aggregating the thin channel to quarterly cohorts to reach a usable size, and says what is lost by doing so
notes that channel cohorts inherit the attribution rule used to assign acquisition channel, and names the rule
expect_fail: ranks the thin channel first or last on its point estimate
drops the thin channel silently
refuses the whole breakdown
